items.question: "The office of the Governor has increasingly become a source of Centre-State friction." Examine the Governor's discretionary powers and the reforms suggested to make the office more impartial.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Governor**, though the constitutional head of the state under **Article 153**, is appointed by the Centre and holds office during the President's pleasure — a design that makes the office a recurring flashpoint in **Centre-State relations**.

**Discretionary powers.** Beyond aid-and-advice, the Governor enjoys real discretion in defined situations: **appointing a Chief Minister** in a hung assembly, **dismissing a CM** who has lost majority, **reserving bills** for the President (Art 200/201), **recommending President's Rule** (Art 356), and, under **Art 163**, deciding conclusively what falls within his discretion. Misuse of these — partisan CM invitations, indefinite withholding of assent, or Art 356 recommendations — has fuelled friction, as seen in *S. R. Bommai* (1994), which made Art 356 justiciable, and the 2023 Supreme Court ruling that a Governor must **return a withheld bill with reasons** rather than sit on it.

**Reforms suggested.** The **Sarkaria Commission (1988)** urged appointing eminent, non-partisan persons in consultation with the CM and using Art 356 as a last resort; the **Punchhi Commission (2010)** recommended a fixed procedure for floor tests, a defined timeline for assent to bills, and provision for the Governor's impeachment by the state legislature. The **Rajamannar Committee** and the Supreme Court have echoed the need for restraint.

**Conclusion.** A Governor acting as a constitutional umpire — not a Centre's agent — is essential for cooperative federalism. Implementing the Sarkaria-Punchhi safeguards, especially timelines on assent and non-partisan selection, would restore the office's dignity and reduce friction with states like Tamil Nadu, Kerala and West Bengal.
keyPoints: Governor is a central appointee (Art 153-156) holding office during the President's pleasure — structural source of friction.
Discretion: CM choice in hung assembly, dismissal of CM without majority, reserving bills (Art 200/201), recommending Art 356; Art 163 makes his discretion final.
S. R. Bommai (1994) made Art 356 justiciable; 2023 SC ruling requires returning a withheld bill with reasons.
Sarkaria (1988): non-partisan appointment, Art 356 as last resort; Punchhi (2010): timelines for assent, floor-test procedure, impeachment by legislature.
Goal: Governor as neutral constitutional umpire to strengthen cooperative federalism.
items.source: NCERT/Laxmikanth — Governor's discretion; Sarkaria & Punchhi Commissions; S. R. Bommai (1994)

items.question: Discuss the composition and utility of the State Legislative Council. In the light of Andhra Pradesh's experience, critically evaluate the debate over its abolition and revival.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad)** is the upper, permanent chamber of a bicameral state legislature under **Part VI**. **Article 169** allows Parliament to create or abolish it on a **special-majority resolution** of the Assembly, and **Article 171** caps its strength at **one-third of the Assembly (minimum 40)**.

**Composition.** It is indirectly constituted: **1/3 elected by MLAs, 1/3 by local bodies, 1/12 by graduates, 1/12 by teachers, and 1/6 nominated by the Governor** — so **5/6 are elected and 1/6 nominated**. As a permanent body, one-third of members retire every two years, each serving six years.

**Utility.** It offers a chamber of **experience and expertise** (graduates, teachers, nominated members), acts as a **revising body** that checks hasty legislation, and gives representation to those unwilling or unable to face direct elections. **Criticisms**: it can only delay, not block, ordinary bills; it is an added expense; and it is often used to accommodate defeated politicians.

**Andhra Pradesh experience.** AP's 58-seat Council is a live case study of Art 169. It existed **1958-1985**, was **abolished in 1985** under N. T. Rama Rao (who viewed it as an obstructive, superfluous body), and was **revived in 2007** under Y. S. Rajasekhara Reddy. Later governments have again mooted abolition, showing how the Council's fate tracks the ruling party's political calculus.

**Conclusion.** The Council's worth depends on how it is used: as a genuine house of review it enriches deliberation, but as a partisan tool it invites abolition. Consistency and merit-based nominations would strengthen the second chamber's legitimacy.
keyPoints: Art 169: Parliament creates/abolishes a Council on the Assembly's special-majority resolution; Art 171 caps it at 1/3 of the Assembly (min 40).
Composition: 1/3 MLAs, 1/3 local bodies, 1/12 graduates, 1/12 teachers, 1/6 nominated — 5/6 elected, 1/6 nominated; permanent body, six-year terms.
Utility: chamber of expertise, revising body, representation for non-electoral talent; criticised as costly, only delaying, and a refuge for defeated politicians.
AP Council (58 seats): existed 1958-1985, abolished 1985 (NTR), revived 2007 (YSR) — a textbook Article 169 illustration.
Council's value hinges on non-partisan, merit-based use rather than political convenience.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — State Legislature (Art 169, 171); AP Legislative Council history (verified online, Sep 2026)

items.question: Explain the principle of collective responsibility of the State Council of Ministers and the constitutional safeguards that limit the size and conduct of the ministry.
items.modelAnswer:
The state executive follows the **parliamentary (Westminster) model**, in which the **Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister** is the real executive that aids and advises the Governor (**Art 163**).

**Collective responsibility.** Under the convention embodied in **Article 164**, the Council is **collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly**. This means the ministry stays in office only while it enjoys the Assembly's confidence; a **no-confidence motion** compels **all** ministers to resign together — including those drawn from the Legislative Council. Ministers must publicly stand by cabinet decisions or resign, ensuring unity and accountability to the popular House. **Individual responsibility** supplements this: ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure, but the Governor removes a minister only on the CM's advice. India, unlike Britain, has **no legal responsibility** of ministers.

**Constitutional safeguards.** The **91st Amendment (2003)** limits the ministry to **15% of the Assembly's strength (minimum 12)** to curb jumbo cabinets, and **bars a member disqualified for defection** from being appointed a minister — reinforcing the **Tenth Schedule**. A non-legislator may be made a minister but must enter the legislature **within six months (Art 164)**. Under **Art 177**, ministers may speak in either House but vote only in their own.

**Conclusion.** Collective responsibility, backed by the 91st Amendment's numerical and anti-defection safeguards, keeps the state executive answerable to the elected Assembly and checks both instability and the temptations of patronage.
keyPoints: State executive follows the parliamentary model; Council of Ministers under the CM aids and advises the Governor (Art 163).
Collective responsibility to the Legislative Assembly (Art 164): a no-confidence motion makes all ministers resign, including MLCs.
Individual responsibility: ministers hold office at the Governor's pleasure but are removed only on the CM's advice; no legal responsibility as in Britain.
91st Amendment 2003: ministry ≤ 15% of Assembly strength, minimum 12; defectors barred from ministership.
Art 164: a non-legislator minister must become a member within six months; Art 177: ministers speak in either House, vote only in their own.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Chief Minister & State Council of Ministers (Art 163, 164, 177); 91st Amendment 2003
